summary:
ireCal Amazonia turns more than two decades of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar for the Brazilian Amazon.

The satellite record is split between MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012). VIIRS detects about 6.1× more hotspots over the same months, so the raw record shows a false jump in 2012. FireCal converts MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent hotspots with factors fitted per 2° tile and month of the year, and validates the result: monthly correlation of 0.99, also 0.99 on years never used for calibration, and total bias reduced from −83% to +0.6%.

An open-source web monitor shows the map, a year × month calendar, anomalies and early-warning indicators for any municipality, state or drawn area. Anyone can rebuild the data and run it locally from the repository.

Team: Vinicius Sarinho, Isaac Fonseca, Daniel Azevedo, Bernardo, Wesley Rios
Code: https://github.com/Repositorio-de-projetos-da-faculdade/nasa-burning-calendar
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FireCal Amazonia turns 20+ years of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar for the Brazilian Amazon. The record is split between MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012); VIIRS detects about 6.1× more hotspots over the same months, so joining them raw shows a false jump in 2012.

HOW IT WORKS

1) Keep vegetation fires with nominal/high confidence. 2) Use one satellite per sensor with the same ~13:30 overpass (Aqua, S-NPP). 3) Count hotspots on a common 0.1° grid (~11 km). 4) Fit a VIIRS/MODIS factor per 2° tile and month of the year on 2012–2021, with shrinkage toward the regional factor where data is sparse. 5) Convert MODIS before 2012; use measured VIIRS after. Result: one unit, VIIRS-equivalent hotspots, 2002 to today.

Validation on 13.4 million hotspots: monthly correlation 0.99, also 0.99 out of sample (2022+, never used to calibrate); bias from −83% to +0.6%. An automated test recovers a planted 3× ratio within 1%.

A web monitor shows, for the biome, any of 9 states or 559 municipalities, or any polygon, radius or coordinates: a map linked to a timeline, a year × month calendar (counts or anomalies), the current month vs. normal to date, year-to-date rank, fire season and record years, plus a Method tab with the validation chart, CSV export and shareable links.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Trends and anomalies become real, not sensor artifacts, for any area with its own historical baseline. Responders see if this month is already above normal; land managers see when their critical period starts; scientists get a long, consistent series. With S-NPP no longer sending data and a strong El Niño under way, we are already adding NOAA-20 the same way to keep the record going.

TOOLS

Python (DuckDB, FastAPI, Shapely, NumPy, PyArrow), TypeScript (React, Vite, MapLibre GL, ECharts), Docker, nginx. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS 375 m), INPE TerraBrasilis, NOAA ONI. No special hardware. Claude (Anthropic) helped with translation, docs and slides.

CREATIVITY

Local factors by region and season instead of one global ratio; matched overpass times; validation shown inside the product; a calendar of squares sharing one heat ramp with the map and timeline, readable at a glance.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Separate calibration and test years; same overpass and official INPE boundary for a fair comparison; color-blind-safe palette; honest limits (clouds and smoke hide fires; hotspots are not burned area); open-source code and public data so anyone can rebuild it.
